Overview

Abstract

Reliable robotic mapping in dynamic real-world environments is essential for embodied intelligence and long-term autonomy. Existing methods face a trade-off: lightweight online mapping captures limited semantic context, while dense mapping provides richer semantics at higher computational cost and can introduce visual distractors. Both struggle when objects move.

We introduce OASIS, an Online Anchor-centric Scene Inference System for online mapping, complex open-vocabulary retrieval, and navigation in dynamic environments. Inspired by the stable structure of indoor scenes, OASIS organizes multimodal memory around semantic anchors such as beds, tables and sofas. An LLM proposes relevant anchors, and a VLM verifies representative views on demand. When a target is missing from its remembered location, transient observations collected during navigation help the robot find it again. Experiments in simulation and a real-world household setup demonstrate improved retrieval and navigation, including relocation after scene changes.

Stable anchors. Rich visual context. A changing world.
OASIS remembers useful views around stable furniture and retrieves the evidence a task needs.

The approach

A scene memory built around anchors

OASIS retains informative views and links them to stable 3D objects.
The same memory supports reasoning, verification and navigation.

01

Curate the memory

Score frames using global scene richness and local anchor quality. Joint spatial and visual clustering retains informative representative views.

02

Retrieve with evidence

The LLM proposes likely anchors. The VLM checks their images for attributes and relations. Class filtering and CLIP matching identify the final 3D instance.

03

Navigate and verify

Return to a recorded observation pose and check the current scene. If the object has moved, search recent observations before proposing another anchor.

When the scene changes

The old location
is only a starting point.

The Transient Visual Buffer preserves potential sightings of moved objects during navigation. Each observation links an object crop to its full contextual frame and camera pose.

  1. Check the remembered location.Compare the current view with visual memory.
  2. Search recent observations.CLIP ranks candidate crops, and a VLM verifies their full frames.
  3. Reason about another anchor.If the buffer has no match, the LLM proposes a plausible place to check.
